newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts dismiss Thai Oct-Dec budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Analysts dismiss Thai Oct-Dec budget gap.

text.p: Economists on Tuesday dismissed Thailand's budget gap during the first quarter of fiscal 1996/97 (October-September) as a temporary phenomenon and said the trend was likely to improve in coming months.

They told Reuters that the jump in expenditure between October-December was caused mostly by heavy reimbursements made during transition of governments late last year and last minute project approvals by the outgoing administration rather than a drop in revenues.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's new government took office in December.
According to a government source, the budget reimbursement for the Ministry of Transport and Communications was one of the biggest among all government agencies.

"This is a freak case. It is unlikely that this spending pattern will continue and the current government should not be blamed for this...They have to work hard to control spending," said Supavudh Saicheua of Phatra Research Institute.

Finance ministry's figures showed that Thailand ran a budget deficit of 53.76 billion baht ($2.08 billion) during October-December of 1996 compared with the surpluses of 16.23 billion baht for the same year-ago period.
Spending in December alone rose 58.73 percent from the corresponding period last year to 86.49 billion baht.
Revenues collected during the first three months of the fiscal year was only 168.45 billion baht while the expenditure reached 222.22 billion baht.
Most of the tax collections during the period fell well below the target, mostly due to a slowdown in the economy.
"We are concerned about below-the-target revenue but frightened by the expenditure which is rather unusual," said Arporn chewakrengkrai of Deutshce Morgan Grenfell.
She added that the trend should improved with lower reimbursements ahead and higher revenue.
Both Supavudh and Arporn expected the tax revenue to rise from the second half of fiscal year and said that would eliminate the shortfalls.

"More revenue from income taxes will be available from March which is the deadline for the payment and corporate taxes will be in between June-July," said Arporn. "But the government must continue its fiscal descipline."
Supavudh said the slowing economy was expected to recover this year and would consequently lead to increased revenues.
"Our opinion is that the economy was bottoming out during October-December. That's perhaps why the shortfalls in revenue was big. The situation should improve this year," he said.
